lessons.title: Sentence structure
lessons.text: A complete sentence normally has a subject and a finite verb. In “The students revise daily”, “The students” is the subject and “revise” is the verb. A fragment such as “After the lesson” does not express a complete main clause.
lessons.q: Which is a complete sentence?

lessons.title: Fractions and proportion
lessons.text: Equivalent fractions represent the same value: 1/2 = 2/4. To add fractions, use a common denominator. For example, 1/2 + 1/4 = 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4. In a ratio, scale every part by the same factor to preserve the relationship.
lessons.q: What is 1/2 + 1/4?

lessons.title: A fair test
lessons.text: A fair test changes one independent variable, measures a dependent variable and controls other relevant variables. When investigating how light affects plant growth, light is the independent variable and growth is the dependent variable. Repeat measurements to assess reliability.
lessons.q: Which variable do you deliberately change?

lessons.title: Particles and states
lessons.text: Solids have particles vibrating around fixed positions. Liquid particles remain close but move past one another. Gas particles are far apart and move freely. Melting and boiling are physical changes: the substance remains chemically the same.
lessons.q: Why can a gas fill its container?

lessons.title: Energy transfers
lessons.text: Energy can be transferred between stores, including kinetic, thermal, chemical and gravitational stores. Total energy is conserved, but some transfers make energy less useful, often by heating the surroundings. Efficiency = useful output energy / total input energy × 100%.
lessons.q: A device uses 100 J and delivers 40 J of useful energy. Its efficiency is:

name: Nigerian Languages
topics: One Nigerian language: Hausa, Igbo, Yoruba or another school-supported language

lessons.title: The Good Samaritan
lessons.text: In Luke 10:25–37, Jesus tells of a Samaritan who helps an injured traveller after others pass by. The story challenges narrow ideas about who counts as a neighbour. Reflect on practical compassion and how you can assist someone in need respectfully.
lessons.q: Which action expresses the central lesson?

lessons.title: The Sermon on the Mount
lessons.text: Matthew 5–7 includes teachings on mercy, peacemaking, prayer and conduct. The Beatitudes describe qualities such as humility and mercy. Study a passage in context, then distinguish what the text says from your personal application.
lessons.q: Which quality is highlighted in the Beatitudes?

lessons.title: Faith and works
lessons.text: James 2:14–26 discusses the relationship between faith and action. The passage uses helping people lacking food or clothing to illustrate practical care. Christian traditions explain the relationship between faith, grace and works in different ways; compare interpretations respectfully.
lessons.q: Which is an example of practical care discussed in this theme?
choices: Offering food to someone in need
Only wishing them well without help

lessons.title: Persuasive writing
lessons.text: Persuasive writing presents a clear claim supported by reasons and evidence. A counterargument fairly describes an opposing view; a rebuttal explains why your claim still stands. Emotional language can engage a reader, but it cannot replace reliable evidence.
lessons.q: What best strengthens a persuasive argument?

lessons.title: Analysing imagery
lessons.text: Imagery evokes sensory experience. A metaphor directly describes one thing as another, while a simile compares using “like” or “as”. When analysing language, quote a short detail, identify the technique and explain its effect in context.
lessons.q: Which expression is a metaphor?

lessons.title: Linear equations
lessons.text: An equation states that two expressions are equal. Keep it balanced by applying the same operation to both sides. For 3x + 5 = 20, subtract 5 to obtain 3x = 15, then divide by 3 to get x = 5. Substitute the answer to check it.
lessons.q: Solve 2x + 4 = 14.

lessons.title: Quadratic equations
lessons.text: A quadratic contains a squared variable. To solve x² − 5x + 6 = 0, factor it as (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0. The zero-product rule gives x = 2 or x = 3. Check each value in the original equation.
lessons.q: What are the roots of x² − 5x + 6 = 0?

lessons.title: Cells and their functions
lessons.text: Cells are basic units of living organisms. The cell membrane controls exchange, cytoplasm supports many reactions, and the nucleus contains genetic material in typical plant and animal cells. Plant cells also have a cellulose wall; photosynthetic cells contain chloroplasts.
lessons.q: Which structure controls exchange with the surroundings?

lessons.title: Photosynthesis
lessons.text: Photosynthesis uses light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen. Chlorophyll absorbs light. Light intensity, carbon dioxide availability and temperature can limit the rate. Plants also respire, including at night.
lessons.q: Which gas is taken in for photosynthesis?

lessons.title: Inheritance
lessons.text: A gene is a region of DNA associated with a functional product; alleles are alternative versions. In a simple dominant–recessive model, Aa shows the dominant phenotype. Two heterozygous parents, Aa × Aa, produce expected genotypes AA, Aa, Aa and aa.
lessons.q: In Aa × Aa, what is the expected probability of aa?

lessons.title: Elements and compounds
lessons.text: An element contains one type of atom. A compound contains different elements chemically bonded in fixed proportions. A mixture contains substances that are not chemically bonded together and can often be separated physically. Air is a mixture, while water is a compound.
lessons.q: Which is a compound?

lessons.title: Balancing equations
lessons.text: Chemical equations conserve atoms. Change coefficients, never formula subscripts, to balance an equation. Hydrogen and oxygen form water: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Both sides contain four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms.
lessons.q: Which equation is balanced?

lessons.title: Moles and mass
lessons.text: The mole is a unit for amount of substance. Calculate amount using n = mass / molar mass. A 18 g sample of water with molar mass 18 g/mol contains 1 mol. Keep units consistent and use the balanced equation for reacting mole ratios.
lessons.q: How many moles are in 44 g of CO₂ with molar mass 44 g/mol?

lessons.title: Speed and motion
lessons.text: Average speed equals distance travelled divided by time taken. A student travelling 120 m in 30 s has average speed 4 m/s. Speed is a scalar; velocity includes direction. Always state units and convert them before calculating.
lessons.q: What is the average speed for 100 m in 20 s?

lessons.title: Forces and acceleration
lessons.text: A resultant force changes velocity. Newton’s second law is F = ma: force in newtons, mass in kilograms and acceleration in m/s². A 2 kg object experiencing a resultant force of 6 N accelerates at 3 m/s².
lessons.q: A 4 kg object has a resultant force of 8 N. Its acceleration is:

lessons.title: Electric circuits
lessons.text: Current is the rate of flow of charge. Potential difference transfers energy per unit charge. For an ohmic resistor at constant temperature, V = IR. With 12 V across a 6 Ω resistor, current is 2 A. In series, current is the same throughout.
lessons.q: What current flows through 6 Ω at 12 V?

lessons.title: Soil and plant growth
lessons.text: Soil provides anchorage, water and nutrients for plants. Sandy soil drains quickly; clay often holds more water; loam combines particle sizes. Organic matter can improve soil structure and water retention. Suitable soil depends on the crop and growing conditions.
lessons.q: Which addition can improve soil structure?

lessons.title: Crop rotation
lessons.text: Crop rotation grows different crops on the same land in successive seasons. It can disrupt some pest cycles and help manage nutrients. Legumes with effective root-nodule bacteria can fix atmospheric nitrogen; residues may contribute nitrogen to later crops.
lessons.q: One benefit of crop rotation is:
choices: Removing the need for all soil management

lessons.title: Integrated pest management
lessons.text: Integrated pest management combines monitoring with cultural, biological and, when appropriate, chemical controls. Identify the pest and assess damage before acting. Use approved products according to their labels and avoid unnecessary pesticide application.
lessons.q: What should come before choosing a pest control?

lessons.title: Sets and notation
lessons.text: A set is a collection of distinct elements. The union A ∪ B contains elements in either set; the intersection A ∩ B contains elements in both. For A = {1,2,3} and B = {3,4}, their intersection is {3}.

lessons.title: Matrices
lessons.text: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers. Add matrices of the same dimensions by adding corresponding entries. The determinant of a 2 × 2 matrix with rows [a,b] and [c,d] is ad − bc. A zero determinant means the matrix has no inverse.
lessons.q: What is the determinant of rows [2,1] and [3,4]?

lessons.title: Differentiation
lessons.text: A derivative measures instantaneous rate of change. The power rule gives d(xⁿ)/dx = nxⁿ⁻¹ for the usual polynomial cases. If y = x³, then dy/dx = 3x². At x = 2, the gradient is 12.
lessons.q: What is the derivative of x³?

lessons.title: Map scale
lessons.text: Map scale relates map distance to ground distance. A scale of 1:50,000 means 1 cm represents 50,000 cm, or 0.5 km. A 4 cm distance therefore represents 2 km. Straight-line distance may differ from distance along a road.
lessons.q: At 1:50,000, what does 2 cm represent?

lessons.title: Weather and climate
lessons.text: Weather describes short-term atmospheric conditions; climate describes patterns over many years. Rainfall, temperature and wind help describe both. A single hot day does not establish a long-term climate trend; use records covering sufficiently long periods.
lessons.q: Which describes climate?

lessons.title: Urbanisation
lessons.text: Urbanisation is an increasing proportion of people living in urban areas. Migration and natural increase can contribute. Cities offer jobs and services, but rapid growth can strain housing, transport and water systems. Compare benefits and challenges using local evidence.
lessons.q: Urbanisation refers to:

lessons.title: The accounting equation
lessons.text: The accounting equation is Assets = Liabilities + Equity. Assets are resources controlled by a business; liabilities are obligations. If assets total ₦100,000 and liabilities total ₦40,000, equity is ₦60,000. The equation remains balanced after recorded transactions.
lessons.q: Assets are ₦100,000 and liabilities ₦40,000. Equity is:

lessons.title: Double-entry bookkeeping
lessons.text: Every transaction has equal debit and credit entries. An increase in an asset is normally a debit; an increase in a liability is normally a credit. Buying equipment with cash debits equipment and credits cash, exchanging one asset for another.
lessons.q: Equipment bought for cash is recorded as:

lessons.title: Profit and cash flow
lessons.text: Profit and cash are different. Gross profit equals sales revenue minus cost of sales. Net profit also accounts for other expenses. Credit sales can increase profit before cash is collected, so a profitable business can still face a cash shortage.
lessons.q: Sales are ₦80,000 and cost of sales ₦50,000. Gross profit is:

lessons.title: Scarcity and choice
lessons.text: Scarcity means resources are limited relative to wants. Choices therefore involve trade-offs. Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative forgone. If you choose study time over your next best option of playing sport, the forgone sporting benefit is the opportunity cost.
lessons.q: Opportunity cost is:

lessons.title: Demand and supply
lessons.text: Demand describes quantities consumers are willing and able to buy at different prices. Other things equal, a higher price usually reduces quantity demanded. A change in the good’s own price causes movement along the demand curve; income or preferences can shift it.
lessons.q: A change in a good’s own price causes:

lessons.title: Inflation
lessons.text: Inflation is a sustained increase in the general price level. It reduces the purchasing power of money. A rise in the price of one item alone is not enough to establish general inflation. Causes can include rising demand or production costs.
lessons.q: Inflation generally reduces:
choices: The number of notes in circulation by definition

lessons.title: Facts and opinions
lessons.text: A factual claim can be checked against evidence. An opinion expresses a judgement or preference. “The survey included 40 students” is checkable; “This is the best school” depends on criteria and viewpoint. Some claims mix fact and opinion, so read carefully.
lessons.q: Which is a checkable factual claim?

lessons.title: Evaluating sources
lessons.text: Evaluate a source by examining its author, evidence, purpose, date and possible bias. Corroboration means comparing a claim with independent sources. A popular post is not automatically reliable; trace important claims to their original evidence.
lessons.q: What does corroboration involve?

lessons.title: Local and global solutions
lessons.text: A global issue can have different local causes and effects. Compare stakeholder perspectives and the likely costs, benefits and unintended effects of proposed solutions. An action plan should identify a goal, responsible people and a way to evaluate results.
lessons.q: Which makes an action plan measurable?
